overview: This two-page U.S. Department of State list of papers inventories reports filed under 894a.20 on military affairs in Japanese-ruled Taiwan from 1933 through the later 1930s. The indexed material traces changes in Taiwan Army command, fortified zones around Keelung and Kaohsiung, restrictions on photography and navigation, attempted transfer of a military map to the American consul, mounting espionage fears, press coverage and correction of the map incident, an intrusion into the U.S. Consulate by an air-raid light-control guard, and Taiwan’s movement onto a war footing during the conflict in China. It also points to reports about aircraft flying from Taipei for raids in China and about military personnel in central and southern Taiwan.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Military Affairs in Formosa (894a.20)
subfiles.about: A two-page index summarizes papers concerning Japanese military organization, defenses, security restrictions, and wartime activity in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The first page indexes reports on Iwane Matsui’s arrival as Taiwan Army commander, a Formosan Chinese man’s attempt to sell Consul Ketcham a map of the Keelung fortified zone, the resulting arrest and adverse press reports, the growing spy scare, navigation restrictions near the Penghu Islands, and regulations against photography. The second page continues with an intrusion into the U.S. Consulate by a light-control guard, the designation of a fortified coastal zone near Kaohsiung, General Motoo Furushō’s succession to Shunroku Hata, and the placement of Taiwan’s defenses on a war basis. It further notes reports of aircraft leaving Taipei to participate in raids in China and an additional, partly garbled entry concerning military personnel in central and southern Taiwan. Several entries cross-reference related State Department decimal files.

interest: The document is valuable as a compact roadmap to a larger body of American consular intelligence on Japanese Taiwan, including papers that may now be dispersed under several decimal-file classifications. It captures the rapid progression from routine reporting on commanders and defense regulations to espionage anxiety, tighter control of information, air operations against China, and formal wartime mobilization. Particularly revealing are the attempted transfer of a fortified-zone map, the official and press response, and the accidental invasion of the American Consulate by a local light-control guard.
